text: Hello, it’s Grete. Today Kirsti wants a fairy tale with a king in it. But Denmark had a real king, and I remember him well. You’ll warm up, work with some words, read Chapter 2, then study one short sentence the way a writer would. Today’s question: what does King Christian the Tenth mean to the Danes?

Today’s reading move is about the gap between then and now. When a character remembers something ordinary from before the war, ask: could that still happen today, on these streets? The space between the memory and the present is where you’ll find the danger.

The model is a short sentence about a king and his horse. The sentence to fix is longer. It joins two complete thoughts with the word and, and it needs a small mark before that word. It also needs a capital on the name for the people of Denmark.

Today’s word work asks you to hunt. In grammar and spelling, more than one answer is hiding in each set, and some of the words that look right are not. Read every word before you tap. Slow and careful wins here.

Last time you lit the bowl of the Big Dipper. Today, four new words light its handle. The roots haven’t changed: one means to break, and one means to lead. Watch the meanings closely. They’ll tell you which root belongs.
Today you match this week’s four words to their meanings. Before you tap, try saying each word in a sentence about Annemarie. If you can use it, you know it. If you can’t yet, the match will help.

Every sentence here has more than one owner-word hiding in it, and a couple of look-alikes with apostrophes. Tap only the words that show who owns something. If a word can be read as two words, like it is, leave it alone.
Most of these words hide a soft, quiet vowel. Today you’re looking for the ones that don’t. Say each word out loud. If every part comes out clear and strong, that’s one to tap.

Today’s Courage Watch is about remembering. King Christian rode his horse through Copenhagen almost every morning, often with no guards at all. My grandmother used to stand on the pavement just to see him pass. Watching him was a way of saying: we still remember who we are. Sometimes courage is simply refusing to forget.

This chapter has a story inside a story. Watch for the moment Annemarie stops telling a made-up fairy tale and starts remembering something true. Notice a famous answer a boy once gave to a German soldier. And notice the sister Annemarie hardly ever talks about.

Today’s sentence holds one moment open. A question has been asked, and instead of giving the answer, the writer shows a girl shaking her head, waiting. That little pause makes you need the next line. When you try it, freeze your character just before the answer arrives.

Now you write. Two questions are about the king and the famous answer the boy gave. The third is about Lise, and that one needs care. Then you’ll turn yesterday’s moment into a claim: one strong sentence that takes a side.

For the second question, the answer the boy gives is short, but it carries a lot. Explain what it means, not just what it says. For the third, two feelings sit side by side in Annemarie. Name both, and find the detail that shows each one.

Yesterday you chose a moment. Today it becomes a claim. A strong claim has three parts: who, which virtue, and exactly how they show it. Look at how Sam sharpens his. Then build yours, one part at a time, and put it together into one clear sentence.

Look at the people on bicycles in this photograph. My grandmother could have been one of them. She told me she would ride out early, just to be on the street when the king came by on his horse. She said he would lift his hand, and for one minute the whole street felt like Denmark again. No guards. Just a king, and his people.
Corrupt. To break down what is good, and make it dishonest.
Bankrupt. A broken bank. Out of money.
Deduct. To lead away, to take an amount off.
Product. Something led forward into being. Something made.
